title: Prostration verses
hookLine: places marked in the mushaf where the reciter prostrates

lines: THE WHOLE ROOM GOES WITH HIM.
cards: The imam is reciting, and the rows behind him stand still, listening. Then, mid-surah, without a word of warning, he goes down: forehead to the floor. The whole room goes with him.
A few seconds later everyone rises, and the recitation carries on as if nothing happened. If you didn't know, you'd be left wondering what you'd missed. You missed a verse that bows.

teach.b: Scattered through the Qur'an are places where the text itself speaks of bowing down: the angels, the stars and the trees, the prophets, the believers who fall down in prostration when the verses are recited to them.
At such places the Prophet ﷺ would prostrate when he recited or heard them. It's called the prostration of recitation, and these are the sajdah verses.
Sajdah means a single prostration, from the same root as masjid, a mosque: the place of prostration. How many are there?
The schools of law count them differently, so the number on the page depends on whose list a copy follows. They also differ on whether it's required.
The Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali schools treat it as a strongly encouraged sunnah; the Hanafi school holds it a duty, wajib, for the one who recites or hears it.

In a printed mushaf the places are marked, often with a line over the key word and a sign in the margin. Bukhari tells how the Prophet once recited Surah an-Najm, prostrated at its end, and those with him prostrated too.
A hadith in Muslim says that when a person prostrates at such a verse, Satan withdraws, weeping, because he was commanded to bow and refused.
The last sajdah in the book closes Surah al-'Alaq, the surah of the first revelation.

In Pickthall's words: "Nay! Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near (unto Allah)." Prostrate, and draw near. Another hadith in Muslim says it plainly: a servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating.
There's even a surah named for it: Surah 32, as-Sajdah.

how: When Muslims recite or hear one of the marked prostration verses, many make a single prostration on the spot, in prayer or outside it, and the whole congregation follows the imam when he does.

o: the name of one surah of the Qur'an
a bow from the waist during prayer
a prostration, forehead to the ground

games.q: verses that bow — tap the pairs.

masjid and sajdah come from the same root

games.q: you're in a mosque. the imam stops in the middle of a surah and goes down to the floor. what do you do?
o: wait for him to get up.
games.why: the congregation prostrates with him at the sajdah verse, then rises, and the recitation carries on.

practice: If you pray, make one prostration, forehead to the floor, and stay there for a few breaths.
If you don't, simply lower your head, or rest your forehead on your hands, and notice what changes when the highest part of you comes to the lowest point.
If a mushaf is near, the mark in the margin at the last verse of al-'Alaq is the easiest one to find.
